Inside Fresno Unified’s Prop. 28-Funded Push for Sustainable Arts Education

The district's $13 million budget largely expanded elementary school arts instruction.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

David Hunter, known for sporting colorful ties printed with art palettes and paintbrushes, is popular among his elementary students. Not only for his eccentric fashion sense, but also because, for many young children in Fresno Unified School District, he is their introduction to the arts.

“Every kid knows who I am and what I’m there to do, and that gives them a lot of joy,” Hunter, a former traditional classroom teacher, said. “They all enjoy having art, and I’m actually there tying it into what they’re learning.”

California’s third-largest school district has dramatically expanded arts education over the past three years, largely due to Proposition 28. The 2022 voter-approved measure sets aside roughly $1 billion annually for California schools to expand the arts for TK-12 students.

But that windfall has brought new challenges for California schools. For decades, arts programs were the first to go with budget cuts. Now, school leaders must quickly spend millions in annual arts funds while navigating a shortage of credentialed arts educators, confusion around spending rules and new standards for art, music, dance and theater programs.

California schools spent about 96% of their Prop. 28 funds from the 2023-2024 school year, the first year of Prop. 28’s rollout, according to the California Department of Education. About 340 school districts, charter schools and county offices of education that did not spend all of their funds will lose a total of $32.9 million in arts education funding next year.

Fresno Unified, with the state’s third-largest allocation of Prop. 28 funds, spent all of its $13 million allocation for the first year. The district hired itinerant instructors to serve all school sites and focused on expanding arts education for elementary schools.

Heather Kuyper-McKeithen, arts education manager for Fresno Unified, said the district zeroed in on two elementary school programs: arts integration (which incorporates the arts into core academic instruction) and dance. Elementary schools must choose to participate in one or the other.

Kuyper-McKeithen said Fresno Unified was able to build its arts programs because it recruited arts teachers early in the rollout of Prop. 28 and educators were “willing to paint the bus while it is going down the road.”

“Everyone was also so used to grant money disappearing after a few years, that we had to think more strategically with an eye towards the long term,” Kuyper-McKeithen told EdSource in October.

Since 2023, Fresno Unified has hired 56 new full-time equivalent arts educators, including 25 full-time dance teachers and 20 elementary arts integration teachers for its 72 elementary schools.

Like a lot of other districts, Fresno Unified has struggled to find enough credentialed arts educators. The district expanded its dance and arts integration programs largely by transferring existing staff into arts teaching roles as they worked to earn new credentials.

Most arts integration teachers, for example, previously taught as traditional classroom teachers and already have multiple-subject teaching credentials. They must earn their supplemental arts credential, or pass the California Subject Examinations for Teachers, within three years on the new assignment.

Many dance instructors also taught under physical education credentials, and can earn their dance credential — which can take up to two years — while teaching in their Prop. 28-funded roles.

Hunter, the arts integration teacher and coordinator at Fresno Unified, helped launch and grow the arts integration program from eight teachers serving 16 schools to 20 teachers serving 40 schools since 2023. Arts integration has gained traction in recent years as a teaching model that may improve learning in core subjects, strengthen retention and support cognitive and social-emotional development by weaving arts into academics.

Hunter previously worked as a classroom teacher and now teaches arts integration lessons in seven elementary classrooms a day between Thomas Elementary and Holland Elementary.

“I’ve been in multiple rooms where students have a hard time engaging with the content, and then, through art, I can help them engage more — that’s stronger than even art as a standalone subject,” Hunter said.

Saima Nunez, a dance teacher at Del Mar Elementary in central Fresno, helped expand the district’s new dance program from four dance instructors teaching at one elementary school to about 25 instructors teaching at 33 school campuses since 2023. She recruited many dance teachers from an existing pool of teaching artists, or non-credentialed instructors who may have taught students outside of regular school instruction.

“Most of the experiences that we were giving (students) were only for kids who were in after-school programs, usually put on by teaching artists, not teaching by the (state) standards,” Nunez said. “Now, they’re getting an actual dance curriculum during their school day. They love it.”

Teacher credentialing remains a barrier

Despite the dance program’s expansion, Nunez, also Fresno Unified’s dance coordinator, said the district has struggled to hire and retain enough dance teachers. Because the state now requires districts to hire instructors with dance credentials, Fresno Unified has lost nine dance teachers since 2023, Nunez said.

“We lose them because the credentialing process is difficult — they’re essentially leaving because they’re not finishing the credentialing, or they’re not getting into the (credentialing) programs,” Nunez said. “Even if we hire them as an intern, if they don’t get into the program, we have to cut them.”…

Michigan Advocates Form Coalition for Paid Leave, Childcare and Higher Wages

The new coalition, called Families Rising, comes as affordability takes center stage in political conversations across the country.

A new coalition of advocacy organizations, pushing for policies that enable a living wage, universal childcare and paid family and medical leave, launched this week as affordability takes center stage in political conversations around Michigan and nationwide.

Jayme Vosovic, the community engagement director at the Michigan League for Public Policy, explained that the coalition, called Families Rising, stemmed from a series of listening sessions hosted around the state by the Michigan League for Public Policy and Michigan United in which participants were asked what makes it hard for their families to get by.

“No matter where we went, the three main issues that kept coming up were jobs with no paid leave, so getting sick or having a baby means losing a paycheck, childcare that costs as much as rent, if you can even find it at all, and wages that haven’t kept up with the price of groceries or rent,” Vosovic said. “We know these are not separate problems. They hit the same families at the same time, and we know that no single organization can fix them alone. So we knew we had to find strength in numbers.”

Leaders from various coalition members spoke about the importance of each of the three policy priorities.

Christina Hayes, a community organizer at Mothering Justice, said that, when talking with mothers and caregivers, they often find themselves “sandwiched” between caring for sick or elderly loved ones and raising their own children, all while employed, demonstrating the need for paid family leave policies.

“Paid leave protects financial security,” she said. “Families should never have to lose their income or risk falling behind on rent, utilities, groceries, while dealing with the family emergency.”

Hayes added that paid leave also acknowledges how many Michigan families serve as caregivers.

“Many residents are caring for aging parents, children with disabilities, or people that are facing serious illnesses,” she said.

Mori Anderson, a mother who said that she lives with kidney failure, explained exactly how important paid leave is for her to be able to survive.

“For me, paid leave is about more than time away from work. It’s about having the freedom to take care of myself, show up for my children, and maintain my livelihood without being penalized for circumstances beyond my control,” she said. “Healthcare equity must include workplace policies that allow for people to actually have access to the care that they need. Navigating a job with a disability should not require sacrificing your health.”

Wende Randall, the director of the Kent County Essential Needs Task Force, said universal childcare has positive impacts for early childhood development by exposing children to environments and social settings outside of their home, as well as in economic stability for families by reducing the pressures that limit the ability of parents to work.

Kermit Williams, the political director of Oakland Forward, added that he hopes to see legislation with a floor of $25 per hour by 2028 — a wage that half of Americans do not make, he said.

“We have people that are working two or three jobs and still qualify for government benefits and assistance right now,” he said. “If we were to put a living wage in Michigan, we would be able not only to raise the economy that we need, but we would be able to make sure that people have time to spend with their families, their loved ones, their kids, pay for sick individuals, and other things that they need in order to survive and thrive.”

Many of the organizations involved with Families Rising have spoken at length since the midterm elections, in which Michigan Democrats won their trifecta on a largely affordability-focused platform, about the need to enact the policies on which officials campaigned on, focused on lowering costs for Michiganders.

Hayes and Randall both noted that the coalition has been in conversations with returning and incoming legislators to find those who are willing to sponsor and champion legislation with these policies, as Democrats prepare to take a trifecta in Michigan’s state government.

“We stay ready, so we don’t have to get ready. So even before the elections were going on, we were watching who was even running, and we already have our elected official champions lined up,” Hayes said.
